hook: This one opens before the report does: a warning screen and a short, melancholy passage you are asked to get through first. Read everything on the page, including the parts that don't look like they belong to the article. The file is about things vanishing, and it uses the page itself to make that feel personal.
whyItMatters: SCP-3309 is metafiction: both its joke and its horror depend on the file being a page on a wiki, with a discussion forum, staff warnings and deletion votes. Its central idea is pointed: anomalies vanish when their files read like weak, overwritten drafts, so the site's own quality standards become a physical force. An Ethics Committee vote then turns that force into the hinge of the story.
thingsToNotice:
Look closely at the list of criteria: overbuilt titanium cells, end-of-the-world stakes with only partial detail, sloppy formatting. It reads like a checklist of complaints about rejected drafts, and the Foundation turns it into a weapon after the tribunal approves it 21 to 20. The test on the Arizona flooding anomaly is staged as a deliberately bad rewrite, complete with an unrelated picture of a wave, and it works.

Then the people start going. Smalls' note drifts from a white hair to locking himself in his office, a colleague is told no Researcher Smalls ever existed, and the colleague's own account is deleted mid-exchange. The ending is a fake discussion thread where Smalls, posting from a place with nothing in it, recalls 3309 erasing staff, task forces, Sites and finally the very concept of an organization, realizes he is one of the erased, and gets warned by an admin for roleplaying while a deletion vote opens. The closing line turns the question on you, the reader, so don't skip those comments.
